I have been farming this 6 mu for 40 years, and I know every inch of it. My wheat went into the ground last October right after we finished the autumn harvest, and now in early spring it is greening up well. With just my wife and me working the land, I cannot afford to try new tricks or chase after fancy methods, so I stick to what has always worked. I buy my wheat seed from the county supply store — it is an improved variety that my neighbors have used for years — and I always plant hybrid maize because the old traditional seeds simply cannot match the yield anymore. Since I have a well, I do not wait for rain; I water when the crops tell me they need it. For the wheat that is already standing, I will spread urea as a top-dressing at the jointing stage and irrigate two more times before we cut it in early June. The minute the wheat comes off, I will run the rotary tiller and plant the maize that same day or the next — in double-cropping, losing even three days to late planting can cost you fifty kilograms per mu. The maize will get compound fertilizer at planting, another shot of urea when the plants reach the big-trumpet stage, and two good irrigations, especially at tasseling. I keep an eye out for weeds and insects, and I spray when I see them, usually twice for each crop. I do not bother with deep ploughing anymore; rotary tillage is enough and saves my back. If the weather does not turn cruel, I expect my wheat to give me about 450 kg per mu and the maize about 550 kg per mu. That will be enough for the two of us and leave some grain to sell.
